metadata.description_blurb: Professor Bear reviews Zhenhao's final project: a verification framework for LLM-generated SQL tested on a Bitcoin blockchain database. The dangerous failure isn’t a crash — it’s a query that runs clean and returns a wrong number. Seven minutes on silent failures, two-path disagreement, property-based testing for SQL semantics, and why the likely negative result is more valuable than most positive ones.

beats.narration_text: Jambo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Zhenhao has a final project idea, and I put one question to Claude: what would Professor Bear say? The project builds a verification framework for LLM-generated SQL, tested on a Bitcoin database, where the dangerous failure isn't a crash — it's a query that runs clean and returns a wrong number. Here is Bear's answer.

props.title: It Ran Clean. It Was Wrong.

beats.narration_text: Act one. The quiet failure.
beats.new_visual_element: SlateCard — Act I title

beats.narration_text: Here's the query. Asked for an address balance, the model sums all outputs paid to that address. It runs. It returns a number. The number has the right shape — looks like a BTC balance. It is ten BTC. The real balance is two.
beats.new_visual_element: ClaudeWindow — SQL query and result (gross vs balance)

props.userPrompt: What is the current balance of address 1A1zP1...?
artifactLines: # Ran clean. 1 row. Nothing signals the error.

beats.narration_text: Bitcoin tracks outputs, not balances. Three received: five, three, two. Two later spent. Current balance: two. SQL summed everything. UTXO counts only unspent. Same question, two different answers — only one tracks the domain correctly.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — UTXO diagram: outputs received, spent flags, gross vs balance

manim.spec: address node on right; three arrows arriving labeled 5 BTC, 3 BTC, 2 BTC; two arrows faded with SPENT mark; one bright (UNSPENT 2 BTC); two result boxes: SQL SUM=10.0 (terracotta, GROSS) vs UTXO balance=2.0 (green, BALANCE)

lines: Gross Received: 10 BTC · Current Balance: 2 BTC

beats.narration_text: A loud failure is manageable. Catch the exception. Flag the empty result. Wrong shape — catchable. Quiet failure is different. The query runs. It returns rows. The shape is right. The value is wrong. And surface plausibility is exactly what's compromised.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — loud failure vs quiet failure

props.title: Two Kinds of Failure

left.label: LOUD FAILURE
left.note: exception · empty result · wrong shape → catchable

right.label: QUIET FAILURE
right.note: runs clean · returns rows · right shape · wrong value

props.sparkLine: Surface plausibility is exactly what’s compromised.

beats.narration_text: A model that fails quietly needs verification that doesn't depend on surface plausibility. Because surface plausibility is the first thing to go. That's the hard part of Zhenhao's project — and it's the right problem.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX still — balance ledger (Tier 1, AI-generate)
beats.prompt: an open accounting ledger with columns of handwritten figures; balance sheet rows; detailed bookkeeping; black and white or sepia; dramatic angled lighting; no people

build.suggested: suggested prompt: an open accounting ledger with columns of handwritten figures; balance sheet rows; detailed bookkeeping; black and white or sepia; dramatic angled lighting; no people

beats.narration_text: Act two. The Bitcoin testbed.
beats.new_visual_element: SlateCard — Act II title

beats.narration_text: Bitcoin is a rare testbed — the same question has two independent computational paths. The SQL path queries a database. The RPC path reconstructs from a live node. When both answer the same question and disagree — that's your error flag, without a human oracle.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — two-path disagreement diagram (SQL vs RPC → FLAG)

manim.spec: center question bubble; two branches: SQL path → database → 10.0 BTC; RPC path → node → 2.0 BTC; comparison at bottom: 10.0 ≠ 2.0 → FLAG (terracotta)

lines: SQL vs RPC — disagreement is the error flag

beats.narration_text: Subtle gotcha: the naive RPC call makes the same mistake. 'getreceivedbyaddress' also returns gross, not balance. Ground truth requires scantxoutset — reconstructing from the UTXO set. Document exactly which calls are immune to the SQL path's failure mode.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — naive RPC vs rigorous ground truth

props.title: Not All RPC Calls Are Ground Truth
props.sparkLine: The cross-validation only works if the two paths fail differently.

beats.narration_text: The independence is the design. Two paths unlikely to be wrong the same way. When they disagree, you know something is wrong — even if neither path tells you what.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX still — distributed network graph (Tier 1, AI-generate)
beats.prompt: abstract network diagram of interconnected nodes; blockchain or distributed ledger visualization; black ink lines on light background; technical illustration style; no people

build.suggested: suggested prompt: abstract network diagram of interconnected nodes; blockchain or distributed ledger visualization; black ink lines on light background; technical illustration style; no people

beats.act: ACT III — Five Types of Failure
beats.narration_text: Act three. The error taxonomy.
beats.new_visual_element: SlateCard — Act III title

beats.narration_text: Run a hundred questions. Inspect every disagreement between SQL and RPC. Let the taxonomy emerge from what you actually find — don't build it top-down. Top-down risks missing the category the system fails at most. Here's what it should look like: five mechanisms.
beats.new_visual_element: ChipGrid — five error types

props.title: Error Taxonomy — Five Mechanisms
props.sparkLine: Build empirically — let cases reveal categories.

beats.narration_text: Type one: semantic misinterpretation. The model knows SQL. It doesn't know UTXO. 'Balance' in accounting means net assets. 'Balance' in Bitcoin means unspent outputs. Right query syntax, wrong domain model — a knowledge gap disguised as a syntax success.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — semantic mismatch: two definitions of balance

manim.spec: word 'BALANCE' at top center; two branches: left box SQL/accounting SUM(all)=10.0; right box UTXO SUM(unspent)=2.0; terracotta gap line between with label 'domain model gap'

lines: Semantic Misinterpretation — Right SQL, Wrong Domain

beats.narration_text: Type four: null swallowing. SQL's SUM silently skips nulls. Missing data looks like zero. For a balance, 'no data' and zero are not the same thing — one is unknown, one is a real answer. The query doesn't warn you which one it returned.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — SQL SUM skips NULLs: table with null values → silent zero

manim.spec: table with 3 rows: 5.0, NULL, 2.0; SUM arrow → 7.0 (NULL skipped, annotated); second scenario: all NULLs → SUM=0 labeled 'no data looks like zero' in terracotta

lines: Null Swallowing — Missing Data Looks Like Zero

beats.narration_text: Types three and five are orientation errors. Type three: a point-in-time snapshot treated as current state. Type five: the model assumed the wrong frame — satoshis versus BTC, or the address's own transactions versus where it appears as a change output.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — temporal confusion and reference frame errors

props.title: Orientation Errors

left.label: TYPE 3 — Temporal Confusion
left.note: snapshot at block N ≠ current state

right.label: TYPE 5 — Reference Frame
right.note: satoshis vs BTC · change outputs vs own txns

props.sparkLine: The model assumed a frame the question didn’t specify.

beats.narration_text: Build the taxonomy empirically. Run first, categorize after. A top-down taxonomy risks missing the category your system actually fails at most. Zhenhao's instinct to let the cases speak first is correct.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX still — hand-drawn taxonomy tree in notebook (Tier 1, AI-generate)
beats.prompt: hand-drawn taxonomy tree or classification branching diagram on paper; pencil or ink; scientific notebook; categories branching from a root; close-up; no people

build.suggested: suggested prompt: hand-drawn taxonomy tree or classification branching diagram on paper; pencil or ink; scientific notebook; categories branching from a root; close-up; no people

beats.narration_text: Act four. The benchmark.
beats.new_visual_element: SlateCard — Act IV title

beats.narration_text: Four tiers. One axis: how many implicit domain assumptions does the question require? Tier one — count transactions in a block. Zero domain semantics. Tier three — current address balance — that's the UTXO problem. Tier four — balance excluding your own change outputs — multi-hop.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — four-tier staircase with implicit assumption counts

manim.spec: four rising steps left to right; T1='Count txns in block X' (0 assumptions), T2='Total ever sent to X' (1 concept), T3='Current balance of X' (UTXO, terracotta highlight), T4='Balance excl. own change outputs' (multi-hop); y-axis: implicit domain assumptions

lines: Four Tiers of Implicit Domain Assumptions

beats.narration_text: Sequencing matters. Compute the RPC ground truth before running the NL-to-SQL system — not after. If you anchor 'correct' on the SQL output first, you bias the sample toward errors that already look wrong, and miss exactly the ones that look right.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — wrong vs correct sequencing

props.title: Sequencing Is the Rigor

left.label: WRONG ORDER
left.note: SQL first → anchor 'correct' on SQL → miss quiet failures

right.label: CORRECT ORDER
right.note: RPC ground truth first → then NL-to-SQL → compare

props.sparkLine: The bias enters before the first query runs.

beats.narration_text: The tiers exist to find calibration patterns — not just to vary difficulty. You want to know if the model is specifically overconfident on state-tracking, not just overconfident in general.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX still — measurement scale or calibration instrument (Tier 1, AI-generate)
beats.prompt: a precision measurement instrument or calibration gauge; technical drawing or photograph; black and white; scientific; no people

build.suggested: suggested prompt: a precision measurement instrument or calibration gauge; technical drawing or photograph; black and white; scientific; no people

beats.narration_text: Act five. Three detection strategies.
beats.new_visual_element: SlateCard — Act V title

beats.narration_text: Strategy one is the backbone: cross-validate against independent computation. Same question, two independent paths. Disagreement flags error. The work is documenting which RPC calls constitute ground truth for each question type — and proving they're immune to the SQL path's failure mode.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — SQL path vs RPC path cross-validation

beats.act: strategy 2: self-consistency and the likely negative result
beats.narration_text: Strategy two: sample the model N times at temp above zero. Execute all candidates. Check agreement. Here's the likely finding — the model fails consistently. All samples make the same UTXO mistake. Self-consistency gives zero signal for the failure this project cares about most.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — N samples all returning same wrong answer (self-consistency fails)

manim.spec: model box at center; five arrows radiating to five output boxes all showing 10.0 BTC; agreement checkmark (5/5 agree); annotation below: 'ALL WRONG' in terracotta; caption 'consistent agreement on a wrong answer'

beats.narration_text: Report that as a finding, not a failure. Sampling-based agreement is not sufficient for systematic semantic errors — that's news. It tells builders something concrete: self-consistency doesn't catch domain-model bugs.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX still — academic findings or research paper (Tier 1, AI-generate)
beats.prompt: a printed academic paper or research findings document; columns of text; abstract visible; scientific journal style; close-up; black and white; no people

build.suggested: suggested prompt: a printed academic paper or research findings document; columns of text; abstract visible; scientific journal style; close-up; black and white; no people

beats.act: strategy 3: differential testing on synthetic DBs
beats.narration_text: Strategy three: a synthetic database where correct and wrong queries must diverge. Three outputs, two spent. Gross received: ten. Balance: two. Run the generated query — if it returns ten, the bug is caught definitively, independent of what real data shows.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — synthetic DB table: 3 outputs, 2 spent → gross=10, balance=2

manim.spec: table: (output 1, SPENT, 5.0 BTC), (output 2, SPENT, 3.0 BTC), (output 3, UNSPENT, 2.0 BTC); two result arrows: SUM all=10.0 (terracotta, GROSS) and SUM unspent=2.0 (green, BALANCE); query returns 10.0 → FLAG 'bug caught'

beats.narration_text: Frame it as property-based testing for SQL semantics — QuickCheck for SQL. The synthetic database is a property test. It's constructed so a semantic wrong answer gives a different number, not just a different shape. That's the rigor the other two strategies can't reach.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — property test framing (QuickCheck for SQL)

props.title: Property-Based Testing for SQL Semantics

right.label: THE TEST
right.note: synthetic DB where the property is violated by construction

props.sparkLine: QuickCheck for SQL — a semantic wrong answer changes the number.

beats.act: ACT VI — Calibration and What Makes It Strong
beats.narration_text: Act six. Calibration and what makes it strong.
beats.new_visual_element: SlateCard — Act VI title

props.headline: Calibration and What Makes It Strong

beats.narration_text: The novel calibration angle is not aggregate overconfidence — that's already known. It's whether the model is overconfident specifically on state-tracking, even if the aggregate curve looks fine. Plot reliability diagrams by tier. A cliff at tier three is the finding.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim — reliability diagram: Tier 1 vs Tier 3 calibration curves

manim.spec: reliability diagram: x-axis stated confidence, y-axis actual accuracy; perfect diagonal (dashed); Tier 1 line near diagonal (green); Tier 3 line above diagonal at high confidence = overconfident (terracotta); shaded gap; legend

lines: By Tier, Not Aggregate — Tier 3 Is the Cliff

beats.narration_text: Three things separate strong from competent. Report the negative result — it's a finding, not a failure. Name one adjacent domain for the generalization claim. Justify the tolerance threshold — rounding noise can masquerade as a semantic error.
beats.new_visual_element: DeckPattern — merely competent vs strong (three differentiators)

props.title: Strong vs Merely Competent

left.label: MERELY COMPETENT
left.note: positive results only · vague generalization · hidden tolerance

right.label: STRONG
right.note: negative results as findings · one named adjacent domain · justified threshold

props.sparkLine: Three moves, each worth a paragraph in the paper.

beats.narration_text: Zhenhao has the right instincts. The project is genuinely novel, the domain is well-chosen, and the likely negative result is more valuable than most positive ones. Ship the taxonomy empirically, report what fails, and the paper writes itself.
beats.new_visual_element: VOX still — research desk with open notebook (Tier 1, AI-generate)
beats.prompt: a research desk with open notebooks and loose papers; overhead or angled view; academic workspace; warm tones; pencils; no people

build.suggested: suggested prompt: a research desk with open notebooks and loose papers; overhead or angled view; academic workspace; warm tones; pencils; no people

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude. It reads: Take Zhenhao's synthetic-database approach and apply it to a domain you know. Pick one natural-language-to-X system where a plausible-looking output can be quietly wrong — SQL, code, calendaring, anything. Design one synthetic test case where the correct interpretation and the plausible-but-wrong interpretation must produce different outputs. What property of the domain makes that construction possible? End quote. The point of that exercise is to find the property that makes quiet failure detectable — the property Zhenhao found in Bitcoin's independent RPC path. Most domains have something equivalent. Find yours.
